idiom_name: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler around a ServeMux or handler
implementation_notes: The Go standard library ships only the endpoint abstraction - http.Handler and the http.HandlerFunc adapter - so the chain is a local idiom: a middleware takes the next handler and returns a new one, and a helper folds a slice of them around the target in reverse so the first middleware is outermost. The FilterManager role is that fold; the FilterChain role is the closure chain. This is the default realization for HTTP services; write the classic object form only when filters need rich configuration that closures express badly.
pitfalls: Forgetting next.ServeHTTP silently swallows the request (an empty 200); the compiler cannot catch it.
A middleware that wraps http.ResponseWriter hides optional interfaces such as http.Flusher or http.Hijacker unless it re-exposes them - use http.ResponseController on modern Go.
Panics in a middleware unwind past the rest of the chain, so recovery middleware must wrap everything it is supposed to protect - its position is part of the contract.

variants.name: gRPC-Go unary/stream interceptors
variants.implementation_notes: For gRPC services the transport owns the request lifecycle, so the chain is built from grpc.UnaryServerInterceptor and grpc.StreamServerInterceptor values, each receiving the decoded request, the method info and a handler continuation, registered with grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor(a, b, ...). Per-RPC metadata is only visible here, which is why auth, tracing and fault injection belong in interceptors rather than in a wrapped net/http handler. Use this variant when the boundary is gRPC and the HTTP middleware idiom would only see bytes.
pitfalls: Interceptors are shared across RPCs: never keep per-call state on the interceptor value; use context values.
A unary-only interceptor leaves streaming methods unguarded - register a StreamServerInterceptor as well.
Chain order is the same contract as any filter chain: authentication must run before anything that logs the authenticated identity.
